entities.name: Baitul Makmur Meulaboh Grand Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Baitul Makmur Grand Mosque (Indonesian: Masjid Agung Baitul Makmur) in Meulaboh, Aceh province, Indonesia, is one of the most historically significant mosques of the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami's aftermath — the Meulaboh mosque was among the relatively few structures that survived the December 26, 2004 tsunami that devastated Meulaboh, killing approximately 40,000 of the town's 50,000 inhabitants. The mosque's survival became a symbol of spiritual resilience and was widely reported in international media coverage of the disaster.

The 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami — triggered by a 9.1-9.3 magnitude undersea earthquake off Sumatra's northwestern coast — is the deadliest tsunami in recorded history, killing approximately 227,898 people across 14 countries. The Indonesian province of Aceh (at the epicenter) suffered the greatest casualties: approximately 130,000 dead or missing in Aceh alone, with coastal towns like Meulaboh virtually destroyed. The mosque's prominent dome structure and reinforced construction allowed it to withstand the catastrophic inundation that flattened surrounding neighborhoods.

Meulaboh and the Baitul Makmur mosque also have significance in Aceh's complex history: Aceh is historically Indonesia's most strictly Islamic province (known as 'Serambi Mecca' — the porch of Mecca), the site of a prolonged separatist conflict (GAM, Free Aceh Movement, 1976-2005 peace agreement), and a province that implemented Islamic sharia law following the post-tsunami autonomy agreement with Jakarta. The mosque's survival in this context carried profound symbolic weight.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Baitul Makmur Grand Mosque Meulaboh — a survivor of the world's deadliest tsunami (2004) that killed 40,000 of 50,000 inhabitants, becoming a global symbol of spiritual resilience — is historically significant as a monument to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami's catastrophic impact and human spiritual endurance.
